data.title: Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi’s remains found in soup pots and fridge, court told
data.description:
Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s remains were stored in two soup pots and a refrigerator after her body was dismembered with an electric saw in a rural village flat, a court has heard.
The High Court trial took a turn towards the end of its fifth week when Choi’s former father-in-law, Kwong Kau, changed his plea to guilty on a charge of illegally disposing of her body. His admission came after the court heard how some of the 28-year-old’s remains were found in Lung Mei village in Tai Po on February 24, 2023.
Kwong, a 68-year-old retired police officer, remains on trial for murder alongside his two sons, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, and Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31. Both sons pleaded guilty to preventing Choi’s burial before the trial began in late September.
Light-hearted exchanges between the judge and lawyers occasionally eased the sombre atmosphere in court, but Deputy Judge Brian Keith reminded the nine-member jury to remain serious throughout the proceedings.
“A young woman died in what was said to be tragic circumstances, and that should not be forgotten,” Keith said.
Detective Constable Chan Wai-hung said police broke into the 600 sq ft rented flat after investigators identified a white Toyota Alphard parked outside as the vehicle used to transport Choi on February 21.
Chan described an “overwhelming” smell of air freshener, similar to that of public toilets, as he entered the flat. Its windows were completely covered with black tape.
In a bedroom covered with blue plastic sheets, police found a plastic box containing a wooden chopping board and what appeared to be human flesh and internal organs, the court heard.
Chan said he later found Choi’s legs in two rubbish bags inside a refrigerator in the living room.

Police also seized two soup pots. One was found to contain Choi’s head when examined at a public mortuary.
Under cross-examination, Chan denied tampering with evidence and said the four colleagues who accompanied him had not touched anything during the search.
Another officer, Sergeant Lam Chun, denied using excessive force when arresting Alex Kwong on February 25 or failing to label DNA samples taken from him properly after his arrest.
Senior government chemist Dr Tam Cheok-ning, a specialist in tool mark analysis, said he found a cut mark on Choi’s remains consistent with the blade of one of two electric saws seized from the flat.
Prosecutors said Choi went missing on February 21 after boarding the Toyota Alphard driven by Anthony Kwong, believing he would take her to Pak Shek Kok to collect her eight-year-old daughter from school.
Alex Kwong allegedly sat beside Choi in the back seat and struck her on the head with a hammer during the journey. Police seized a one-pound ball-peen hammer from the village flat three days later.
A hardware shop employee in Kowloon City confirmed that the hammer seized from the flat was the one he sold to Anthony Kwong on February 15.
In a written statement, Alex Kwong’s friend and former business partner Herman Ng Deng-hao said the defendant had asked to borrow a car in January 2023. Kwong said his own car was booked in for maintenance and he needed a vehicle to drive his children to school.
Ng referred Kwong to his own elder brother, who lent the latter a seven-seater Toyota Alphard. Kwong allegedly used the vehicle to transport equipment for dismembering Choi’s body after she was killed. It was not the Alphard she had used.
The statement also shed light on Alex Kwong’s apparent affluent lifestyle while he was living in mainland China and evading criminal proceedings in Hong Kong over a HK$6.3 million theft case.

He said Kwong appeared wealthy during his time on the mainland, staying at the luxury Rosewood Guangzhou hotel and using a personal driver to travel around the province in either a Rolls-Royce saloon or a seven-seater Lexus.
But whenever they met for meals, Ng noted, Kwong appeared to use mobile payment apps authenticated under the abbreviated names “Fung” or “Tin-fung”.
Ng said Kwong was forced to return to Hong Kong on June 10, 2022, after telling Choi he had a girlfriend.
According to Ng, the influencer was upset that her ex-husband was “picking up girls” on the mainland while neglecting their two children in Hong Kong.
Prosecutors allege the murder stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million (US$9.2 million) flat at the upmarket Kadooria residential estate in Ho Man Tin.
Kwong Kau, the flat’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi’s efforts to sell it and enlisted his two sons to help kill his former daughter-in-law and dispose of her body.
The court heard that the elder Kwong signed a power of attorney on November 7, 2022, authorising Choi to negotiate the sale after her mother threatened to take him to court.
Two property agents who were contacted by Choi in November 2022 and February 2023, respectively, testified that she was eager to sell the flat. They said no prospective buyers had made inquiries about it before her death.
The trial continues.

data.title: Evergrande liquidators strike US$513 million deal to sell property services arm
data.description:
Liquidators of China Evergrande Group have agreed to sell a controlling stake in its property management arm to investment firm PAG for HK$4.03 billion (US$513.6 million), as they seek to recover assets for creditors owed US$46 billion.
The sale of a 51.016 per cent stake in Evergrande Property Services could give the profitable business a new controlling shareholder after its parent used billions of yuan of its bank deposits as collateral for loans, leaving the company struggling to recover the money.
PAG, a Hong Kong-based investment firm, would acquire about 5.52 billion shares from China Evergrande and CEG Holdings, both in liquidation, according to a joint announcement on Friday.
“Following an extensive and competitive sale process, we are pleased to have been able to conclude this agreement with PAG, the completion of which will enable [Evergrande Property Services] to move onwards into a renewed phase of growth,” liquidator Eddie Middleton said in a statement to the South China Morning Post.
Further work was required before the transaction could be completed, Middleton added.
PAG will pay HK$0.8359 per share for China Evergrande’s 147.16 million shares and HK$0.7271 per share for CEG Holdings’ 5.37 billion shares. The transaction remains subject to conditions, including regulatory approval in mainland China.
Upon completion, PAG will be required to make an unconditional mandatory cash offer for the remaining shares at HK$0.8359 apiece. The offer price is 29.5 per cent below Evergrande Property Services’ closing price of HK$1.185 on October 28, the last trading day before the announcement.
Following a brief suspension ahead of the takeover announcement, the company resumed trading on Friday.
PAG said it intended to maintain Evergrande Property Services’ Hong Kong listing and did not plan any major operational changes beyond board-level adjustments, according to the statement.
The property manager provides services across mainland China and reported revenue of 6.94 billion yuan (US$1 billion) and net profit of 503 million yuan in the first half of 2026.
Its finances, however, have been caught in its parent’s collapse. China Evergrande used 13.4 billion yuan of its bank deposits as collateral for loans. By June, Evergrande Property Services had recovered just 9.5 million yuan from its parent and other parties, according to its interim report.
China Evergrande defaulted on its offshore debt in 2021 and was ordered to wind up by Hong Kong’s High Court in January 2024. Its liquidators had recovered US$435.9 million through asset sales and loan recoveries, less than 1 per cent of the US$46 billion in creditor claims, according to their second progress report published earlier this month.

data.title: From digital pets to robot pals: how AI is changing Hong Kong classrooms
data.description:
Hands shot up in a Hong Kong Primary Two classroom as pupils debated what their digital pet needed more, meal vouchers or the latest game cards.
Their teacher at SKH Kei Oi Primary School in Sham Shui Po had created the virtual pet using artificial intelligence (AI) and web tools for a lesson on saving and budgeting.
With each spending decision, the pet’s mood and savings changed on screen, helping pupils discover the consequences of careless spending.
Such lessons are becoming more common across Hong Kong, where about 60 per cent of primary and secondary schools use AI in teaching or administration, according to an Education University of Hong Kong survey released in June.
Supported by a government blueprint for digital education and a HK$500,000 (US$63,733) grant for each publicly funded school, schools are developing their own AI platforms or working with industry to adapt the technology to their students’ needs.
AI has helped teachers plan lessons and overcome barriers to learning. But teachers said assessing students’ AI-assisted work required more training, while principals called for closer collaboration between schools and industry to support pupils with special educational needs.
The Education Bureau released its Blueprint for Digital Education Development in June, requiring teachers to complete at least 30 hours of digital training every three years and directing schools to incorporate AI strategies into their annual development plans.
The bureau has also provided a one-off HK$500,000 grant to every publicly funded primary and secondary school through its AI for Empowering Learning and Teaching Funding Programme, launched in 2025. The money can be used to buy or lease AI software, hardware and platforms, and to fund activities that develop students’ AI literacy.
SKH Kei Oi Primary School has adopted both off-the-shelf and custom-built AI tools, initially focusing on science and English for Primary Four to Six pupils.
Ready-made applications include image generators that turn pupils’ English compositions into comics, as well as platforms that assess their speaking and writing skills.
Principal Szeto Kar-ying said finding suitable products in a crowded market was not easy, but the school’s guiding principle was to put teaching needs ahead of the latest technology.
When no suitable product is available, the school works with industry to develop its own solution.
With support from a programme run by the bureau and Cyberport, it partnered with a technology company to create an AI-driven science reading platform that guides pupils through texts and concepts.
“Funding goes first to projects that fit curriculum needs and can be sustained and scaled up. We also encourage our teachers to experiment with AI in everyday teaching and classroom activities,” Szeto said.
Teacher Cynthia Doo Chi-yin’s budgeting game, in which her Primary Two humanities class manages a digital pet’s monthly spending, is one example of teachers developing their own AI teaching tools.
“I make the spending choices together with them in class. They are excited to explore it first-hand and discover on their own that irrational spending has consequences, affecting the character’s mood,” she said.
While AI has opened up new possibilities for lesson design, it has also made assessing students’ abilities more challenging.
“If we only assess the final product, students can easily get AI to do the work for them. Assessment should value the process over the result and cover how students collaborate with AI, not just test their knowledge,” said Chan Yuk, the school’s IT coordinator.
He said this approach added to teachers’ workloads, and schools needed to provide training and time rather than leaving staff to work it out themselves.
Dragan Gasevic, chair professor in the Faculty of Education and the School of Computing and Data Science at the University of Hong Kong, said assessments now needed to shift their focus from the final product to the process behind it.
“When a sprinter races, the coach does not just record the finishing time. They replay the whole race step by step to find the moments where performance could improve,” he said.
“We need tools that let teachers and students replay these steps too, and identify the points of weakness when students interact with AI.”
Such tools should be co-designed with children and teachers, he said, with students given control over their own data and schools fostering a coaching culture.
Gasevic said schools needed to distinguish AI designed for education from general-purpose AI.
“Real learning gains require specialised adaptive systems, not simply asking ChatGPT or Gemini to run a Socratic dialogue. These systems, built on more than 50 years of research in AI in education, need components that adapt to the individual needs of each student,” he said.

For students with special educational needs, AI can help overcome learning barriers by responding to their emotional needs and offering alternatives to typing, such as pictures and voice input.
Hong Chi Winifred Mary Cheung Morninghope School, which caters to children aged six to 18 with intellectual disabilities, has introduced various robots as learning companions.
Principal Chu Pui-man said the school had invested in smart devices and AI platforms to immerse students in technology and help them become confident using it in daily life beyond school.
“We bought two humanoid robots that students can learn to programme, and they once led the whole school in morning exercise,” she said.
“In our classrooms we keep more than 10 companion robots, our AI learning buddies, which chat with students when they feel unhappy and comfort them.”
The school has also partnered with a technology company to create an AI avatar that serves as an assistant on students’ tablets. Because commercial products do not meet all its students’ needs, it maintains an in-house team to develop a school-based platform.
“Our students might not speak fast or clearly, so we need to adjust the platform to their pace, guide them step by step and not rush ahead, and allow them to enlarge the text. We also preset question choices on the platform for students who cannot type,” she said.
She added that AI also allowed students to ask questions through images or speech rather than using a conventional keyboard.
But customising and trialling AI products took additional time and money.
“We hope to see cross-school resource sharing and centralised procurement for special education, so schools do not each end up buying the same thing at a high price,” she said.
“If the tech industry could recommend well-tested products and explain why they suit our students, we could save time searching and customising on our own.”
The task of matching products to schools falls partly to Hong Kong Education City (EdCity), the government-funded education portal.
Launched in 2000 to promote the digitalisation of education, EdCity has evolved in recent years from primarily a repository of digital content into a platform connecting technology companies with schools as AI use grows.
Its executive director, Dr Tenny Lam Fung, said schools could draw on AI solutions from around the world. For mainstream schools, the challenge lay in choosing the right ones.
“Mainstream schools have many choices. The question is which one to pick, how to use it, and how to get clear feedback. We provide a platform, EdMarket, for schools and companies to share their successful cases and help schools choose,” he said.
For special schools, the challenge worked both ways: schools had fewer suitable products to choose from, while companies struggled to reach the right classrooms.
“Students with special needs have many different learning needs, and it is very hard for one solution to meet them all. So the challenge for special schools is how to find the right solution for each application context,” he said.
He added that EdCity had stepped up support for special schools, including through an AI in Education Forum co-organised with the Education University of Hong Kong, at which special education researchers present their work.
Lam described the digital education blueprint as an important milestone in setting the overall direction but said choosing solutions was a matter of implementation for schools and the Education Bureau.
“The blueprint sets out the framework, principles and policies. It will not go into detail on how to choose solutions. That is where execution comes in, and that is the role we play,” he said.
“In execution, things must keep evolving as technology updates. But some principles will remain unchanged: people first, technology for good and using technology responsibly.”

data.title: AI, fuelled by advanced chips, set to power their manufacture: industry veteran
data.description:
Artificial intelligence is no longer merely the driving force behind global semiconductor demand, but is also actively reinventing how chips are designed and built, industry leaders and scientists said at a major science forum in Shanghai on Friday.
Chen Yunji, co-founder of AI chipmaker Cambricon Technologies, predicted that the integration between AI and chip design would eventually automate the chip design process entirely.
“In the [next] 10 years, the most important development … is the RSI (recursive self-improvement) techniques for artificial intelligence, where AI models improve AI models, and AI chips improve AI chips,” Chen said.
“With the potential of RSI, it is possible that one day AI systems will autonomously design better chips, which leads to better AI systems in a self-recursive loop.”
The transformation is already reaching the factory floor, according to the speakers. Lu Guangquan, chairman of Chinese semiconductor equipment maker Piotech, said industrial AI had evolved from generating text to executing physical fabrication processes.
With front-end manufacturing tools accounting for over 80 per cent of fabrication costs, Chinese foundries were increasingly deploying AI-powered digital twins and predictive models to improve chip equipment engineering and operations, and eventually boost wafer yields, Lu said.
The remarks, delivered at the 2026 World Laureates Forum, underscored how China’s chip sector is embracing AI to overcome domestic manufacturing bottlenecks and drive automation across the entire supply chain.
The shift comes as AI shapes the architecture of scientific computing. Jack Dongarra, an American computing pioneer and Turing Award winner who also addressed the forum, said AI was forcing those in the industry to rethink processor design.

“AI does not simply add another workload to high-performance computing; it also changes the hardware that scientific computing will have,” Dongarra said, noting that AI workloads depended less on 64-bit FP64 calculations and placed greater strain on memory bandwidth and energy across systems.
FP64 is a 64-bit double-precision floating point, the mathematical format that most scientific simulations and supercomputing benchmarks rely on.
Beyond the production line, the technology was reshaping how China trained its next generation of chip engineers, experts said.
Wu Hanming, director of the Information Science Division at Zhejiang University, said the university’s integrated circuits college was using AI systems such as FabGPT alongside simulation engines. The set-up created virtual fabs where students could experience CMOS production lines digitally, he said.
But even as AI automated code and semiconductor layouts, it remained dependent on hardware to perceive the real world, according to Liu Sheng, dean of the School of Integrated Circuits at Wuhan University.
Liu highlighted surging demand for smart sensors and micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) in humanoid robotics and autonomous driving.
“Sensors are the foundation … acting as the link between the physical and information worlds,” Liu said, adding that developing advanced packaging and testing platforms was critical to keeping complex MEMS chips reliable and cost-effective.

data.title: On This Day|Fire at Hong Kong’s Jumbo Floating Restaurant kills 34 in 1971 – SCMP archive
data.description:
This story was first published on October 31, 1971.
Aberdeen was yesterday (October 30, 1971) rocked by a tremendous explosion followed by fire which swept through the $14 million Jumbo Restaurant, killing 13 and injuring at least 42 others on board.
It happened so quickly that within five minutes, fire engulfed the four-decked floating restaurant, reducing it to a charred hulk.
Hundreds of people leapt for life from the decks and from the pagoda-shaped towers of the palatial restaurant.
It was a frantic scene of struggle for survival which grasped boat people and weekend yachtsmen nearby who watched in horror.
The news of the fire and the high toll shocked Aberdeen.

Just how hard the blow was to the fishing community could not be immediately ascertained, as a large number of the casualties are believed to come from Aberdeen itself.
Cause of the high toll was the presence on board of 200 painters, welders and workers putting the finishing touches for the opening of the restaurant scheduled for November 17.
The Chief Fire Officer, Mr H. T. J. Hutchins, who directed the fire fighting operations, attributed the high toll to the rapid spread of the fire, coupled with a series of explosions, and the difficulties in getting out.
“The only exit is jumping into the sea,” the Chief Officer, Hongkong, said.
The water was full of bobbing heads, and boats of all descriptions rushed to pick them up.
One of the early parties who dashed to the scene was six police officers from Aberdeen.
They were Detective Inspector James Bruce, Blue Beret Inspector P. M. Mullens, and Detective Inspector L. Burton, Cpl Lam Kam-yat and two constables.
They spotted the fire from the station, and rushed to nearby boats for the rescue.
“A dozen of them were clinging to the sides of the Jumbo restaurant,” Insp Bruce said.
“They were badly burned and were shouting for help,” he said.
After picking up these survivors, the police officers continued the rescue work in the vicinity picking up more people.
Several sampans near the floating restaurant were not spared from the holocaust.
Four children of a boat family were burned to death when their craft caught fire and was completely gutted.
Their grief-stricken father, Wong Fat-hoi, 46, told the police of the tragedy after he helped his wife ashore.
The children were left on the boat when Mr Wong and three other members of his family were ashore.
When he and his wife heard of the fire, they rushed back only to find the four had perished.
Mrs Wong who collapsed on hearing the news was rushed to hospital.
A fisherman, Mr Chan Kan-tai, 23, tried desperately to row to his boat where his mother-in-law and several children were but the intense heat and leaping flames forced him to turn back.
The family had all jumped safely into the water, and only his mother-in-law was hurt with burns in the back, Mr Chan later learned.

Mr Chang Ching-sing, one of the restaurant’s stewards who escaped, said the fire broke out at the stern on the lowest deck of the ship at about 3 pm.
Welding was being carried out in the section of the ship, he said.
The fire quickly swept through the whole craft.
“Everyone had to jump as the fire was burning fiercely,” he said.
A yachtswoman who witnessed the start of the fire, said many workers on the upper decks who went to the stern to have a look soon found themselves trapped as the fire rapidly spread upwards.
Mr Hutchins said his men removed 61 casualties to hospital. Police launches might have picked up more, he said.
He believed the fire started as a result of an explosion apparently from a large quantity of oil and a number of oxy-acetylene tubes on board.
Investigations into the disaster had already begun, Mr Hutchins said.
The Acting Governor, Sir Hugh Norman-Walker, last night sent his sympathy to the families of the victims.
In a message from Government House, Sir Hugh said he was shocked to learn of the tragic news.

data.title: CATL, Gotion to gain as oil prices drive energy-storage demandBattery systems see strong demand from solar projects in Middle East and Southeast Asia as China’s dominant makers accelerate delivery.
data.description:
China’s makers of energy storage systems, including Contemporary Amperex Technology (CATL) and Gotion High-Tech, stand to benefit as conflict in the Middle East keeps fossil fuel prices elevated, raising demand for their products in green energy projects, according to analysts.
The tailwinds are expected to outweigh a slowdown in the local market, where weaker-than-expected demand has dragged stock prices in the lithium-ion battery supply chain down by more than 46 per cent over the past six months.
Amid the war in the Middle East, demand had risen for battery energy storage system (BESS) products in the Middle East and Southeast Asia, said Lucas Zhang Liutong, director of Hong Kong-based consultancy WaterRock Energy Economics. Solar and wind projects relied on BESS, and Chinese companies dominated the market, Zhang added.
“Economically, solar plus BESS for 24/7 operation can be cost competitive against new liquefied natural gas-fired combined-cycle gas turbine projects in Asia,” he said. “Thus, in countries with sufficient space for large-scale solar projects, demand for [Chinese] BESS is expected to increase materially in the coming years.”
In the first half of the year, Chinese BESS integrators accounted for nine of the world’s top 10 providers of such products by shipments, with Shenzhen-based BYD leading the pack, according to Taipei-based consulting firm InfoLink.
By the volume of energy storage batteries, CATL led nine other Chinese manufacturers, as the country’s producers occupied the entire top 10 during the same period, data from Seoul-based SNE Research showed.
Besides cost advantages, Chinese companies can leverage their high product quality and fast delivery to capture new demand overseas, said Yale Zhang, managing director of Shanghai-based consulting firm Automotive Foresight.
“Only Chinese companies have the technical talent and dedicated teams capable of handling stable, long-term plant operations and maintenance that could last over 20 years,” he added.
Gotion and BYD have reduced delivery timelines for some overseas projects to three months from five to seven months earlier.
For example, Gotion sent the first batch of BESS products for Africa’s largest stand-alone project only three months after a signing ceremony, according to a statement from the company. The first 50 trucks departed for the project in Egypt at the end of September, said the company, based in Hefei, the capital of central China’s Anhui province.
BYD broke ground on Poland’s largest manufacturing facility for battery storage systems in late September with partner Greenvolt Group. With a planned capacity of 2.4 gigawatt hours, the commercial operation is expected to start by the end of 2027.
Zhang of WaterRock warned that shortened timelines from signing to delivery could indicate BESS overcapacity and high competition among Chinese companies in overseas markets.
CATL pushed back against oversupply warnings in its earnings call on October 21, saying that it expected BESS demand in international markets to “remain robust” next year.
Overall, the global demand for batteries might not be as pessimistic as the market had worried, with relatively good growth potential, executives of the world’s leading producer of batteries for electric vehicles told investors after the firm reported a sharp slowdown in its third-quarter net profit.

data.title: Would you buy a death-linked flat? Hong Kong, France give very different answers
data.description:
Even as Hong Kong remains the world’s least affordable housing market, many buyers still shun heavily discounted homes linked to an “unnatural death”, such as murder or suicide, according to property agents.
Prices for such properties could fall by as much as 50 per cent, while rents were typically about 20 per cent below market rates, they added.
The aversion stands in stark contrast to parts of Europe, particularly in France, where buyers are often willing to purchase homes under a “vente en viager” arrangement that can see properties sold at discounts of up to 80 per cent below market value.
Under the system, an elderly homeowner agrees to sell a property in exchange for an upfront payment and a monthly annuity that continues for the rest of their life.
The arrangement allows sellers to supplement their retirement income while remaining in their homes. For buyers, the main attraction is the steep discount, even if they may have to wait for years before taking possession.
In effect, buyers are betting on how long sellers will live before they can claim the property.
“In Hong Kong, there is no official definition or registry for ‘haunted houses,’ or xiong zhai in Chinese,” said Ivy Wong, managing director of Centaline Mortgage.
“The term generally refers to properties associated with unnatural deaths, such as murders, suicides or fatal accidents, which are distinctly separated from natural deaths such as passing away from old age.”
The “haunted houses”, particularly those linked to sensational murder cases, could receive a zero valuation or be deemed ineligible for valuation, making it difficult to secure a mortgage, according to Eric Tso Tak-ming, chief vice-president at mReferral Mortgage Brokerage Services.
“Because the difficulty of reselling these properties in the future is exceptionally high, valuation firms significantly reduce their valuations,” Tso said. “Consequently, it is very difficult for banks to approve the buyer’s desired loan amount, and they often lower the loan-to-value ratio.”
Recently, a low-floor flat with a private podium in Metro Town in Tseung Kwan O was sold for HK$4.5 million (US$574,000), significantly below the more than HK$7 million valuation for a comparable home on a similar floor in another tower of the same project.
The reason, according to one agent, was that a person had fallen from a higher floor and landed on the flat’s private podium, stigmatising it as a “haunted house”.
Murders, especially those involving multiple victims, grisly details or extensive media coverage, tend to have the most severe impact on home assessments and could result in outright mortgage rejections
Ivy Wong, Centaline Mortgage
In some cases, online mortgage valuation platforms operated by banks do not generate valuations for homes associated with such incidents.
There were also cases where the “negative impact even spilled over, causing online valuations for the entire floor to become unavailable”, Centaline Mortgage’s Wong said.
Banks and surveying firms relied heavily on internal databases and media reports of tragic incidents to conduct case-by-case assessments, she added.
Banks, however, do not all take the same approach. “While some adopt a highly conservative approach and outright reject mortgage applications for stigmatised properties, the majority rely on individual assessments to determine approval and set conditions,” Wong said.
Assessments depend on factors including the nature and severity of the incident. Murders, especially those involving multiple victims, grisly details or extensive media coverage, tended to have “the most severe impact” and could result in “outright mortgage rejections”, she said.
Suicides involving charcoal burning, jumping or hanging, as well as fatal accidents such as falls or gas explosions were generally viewed as less severe, and more open-minded banks could still consider mortgage applications for such properties, Wong added.
Valuations for homes linked to high-profile murder cases would typically fall by 50 per cent or more, while those associated with suicides or fatal accidents could decline by at least 30 per cent, she said.
However, if an incident occurred decades ago and the property had changed hands or been leased multiple times since, some banks could “view the negative impact as diluted, resulting in a more favourable assessment”, Wong said.
France and several other European countries, including Belgium, Switzerland, Spain, Italy and Germany, take a markedly different view of death in relation to property transactions under the “vente en viager” arrangement.
“What sets France apart is how common private, person-to-person ‘viager’ sales are, with a well-developed legal framework around them,” said Alex Balkin, head of Savills French Riviera.
The arrangement offered advantages to both sellers and buyers, Balkin added.
For sellers, the benefits included additional retirement income while remaining in their homes, annuity payments indexed to inflation and part of the income receiving a “favourable tax treatment”, he said.
Sellers were also well-protected, as contracts typically contained clauses allowing them to reclaim the property and retain payments already received if buyers stopped paying.
For buyers, the property’s price was discounted to reflect occupancy and the seller’s life expectancy, while payments were spread over time, removing the need for a traditional bank mortgage, according to Balkin.

Some Hong Kong-based buyers had inquired about purchasing French property through a “vente en viager” arrangement, said Sebastien Salin, a Hong Kong-based French entrepreneur and the founder of Acheterpourlouer, a real estate advisory firm that helps expatriates and foreigners to buy properties in France remotely.
“There’s a number of clients who have shown an interest, but it’s a limited percentage,” Salin said.
Depending on the seller’s age, discounts could reach as much as 80 per cent of market value, he added.
“This arrangement is getting more popular because a lot of people are getting older and don’t have much income, but they have a nice flat,” Salin said. “So they want to get some extra funds to make sure they have enough income during the remaining years of their life.”
There is, however, a famous example of a transaction that went badly wrong for the buyer.
In 1965, Jeanne Calment sold her home in Arles, France, at age 90 under a “vente en viager” arrangement to Andre-Francois Raffray, a 47-year-old lawyer.
Raffray paid Calment 2,500 French francs a month for 30 years before dying in 1995. His widow continued the payments until Calment died in 1997 at the age of 122. By then the family had paid more than twice the home’s value, according to Savills. France replaced the franc with the euro in 1999, when 2,500 francs equalled around US$405.
“It’s a little bit like gambling,” Salin said.
In Hong Kong, the aversion to properties linked to unfortunate circumstances stemmed from “the prevailing cultural beliefs and superstitions that are deeply ingrained in local Chinese society,” according to a spokesman from Centaline Property Agency.
There were, however, prospective buyers or tenants willing to consider these properties, he said.
“Individuals who do not subscribe to local superstitions, such as Catholic buyers, expatriates and atheists, are much more open to living in these homes,” he said.
“This is particularly driven by budget constraints or a desire to save money, as the significant rental discounts of around 20 per cent below standard market rates make these properties a highly cost-effective option.”
Even so, the long-term value of these properties generally does not fully recover or keep pace with the broader property market.
“While general market growth may result in a slight increase in value, these properties almost invariably continue to trade at a significant discount relative to comparable, unaffected properties in the same neighbourhood,” the spokesman said.

data.title: Exclusive|Bordeaux officials hail exclusive 5-year deal for Hong Kong to host Vinexpo
data.description:
Having a presence in Hong Kong and the rest of China is “very important” for Bordeaux, an official from the world-renowned French wine-producing region has said, even as consumption declines on the mainland.
The comments by deputy mayor Fabien Robert came as Vinexpo, a premier international wine and spirits trade exhibition that began in Bordeaux, signed a deal for its Asian edition to be hosted solely by Hong Kong from 2027 to 2031.
“To be in Hong Kong every year, I think it’s a message ... [to] Asia and China about the seriousness of Bordeaux wine. We are in Asia, we are in China, in Hong Kong, and this is very important for Bordeaux,” Robert said in an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post on Friday.
Vinexpo Asia alternated annually from 2023 to 2026 between Singapore and Hong Kong when it returned after the Covid-19 pandemic. The memorandum of understanding ends the dual-city rotation from next year.


“It’s like fidelity between Bordeaux and Hong Kong,” Robert said. “We have a long story in the past and we have a long future … the two cities are very different … but we have the same ambition … with gastronomy, and this point is very important to have Vinexpo here every year.”
Laure Compeyrot, Bordeaux’s municipal councillor and delegate for wine industry relations and wine promotion, said that while Vinexpo also had access to the Hong Kong market before, being in the city permanently was different.
“When you meet people every year, something is stronger. It’s like with your family. You need to be together very often, and you need to meet each other and to share and to speak and to understand each other. That is so important,” she said.
China’s per-capita wine consumption peaked in the mid-2010s, while sales plunged 47 per cent between 2019 and 2022, according to a study published last year by University of Adelaide economist Kym Anderson.
By volume, China’s bottled wine imports from the European Union fell 16.6 per cent year on year in the first half of 2026, according to Chinese customs data, with their value dropping by 7.9 per cent to US$251 million. Shipments from France fell 14.3 per cent.
A report released by the Paris-based International Organisation of Vine and Wine in May said global wine consumption had fallen 14 per cent since 2018, with China recording the largest contraction among major markets.


“Exportation to China was a little [lower]. It’s necessary not [just] to have more wine, more exhibitions, confidence is very important in commerce for stability,” Robert said, pointing to the fair’s commitment.
“When you have something a little bit less, you have to work more and to share more and to speak more,” Compeyrot said, adding that enhanced exposure would help.
Beijing has imposed anti-dumping duties of about 30 per cent on European brandy, mostly French cognac, in a move seen as retaliation for a European Commission decision to impose steep anti-subsidy tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles.
Robert said he was not worried about geopolitics potentially affecting the wine trade, adding that it was difficult to make predictions and he was adopting a wait-and-see approach, while stressing his ambition to trade with Asia.
Asked if wine could serve as a lubricant in otherwise tense relations between the two countries, Compeyrot said “of course” without hesitation. Robert indicated that wine and gastronomy were important soft powers.
“With wine you don’t transmit only the [drink], you transmit the culture and civilisation,” he said, adding that it helped people understand each other.
“You don’t speak the same language, but you drink the same wine, and this is a part of comprehension.”

data.title: UK minister discusses tech collaboration in Greater Bay Area during Hong Kong visit
data.description:
UK Indo-Pacific minister Rosie Winterton has visited Hong Kong’s flagship tech hub to discuss plans to expand technological collaboration in the Greater Bay Area, while aiming to strengthen business, education and people-to-people partnerships with the city.
During her visit, Winterton also raised concerns about the jailing of former media boss Jimmy Lai Chee-ying in talks with Cui Jianchun, Beijing’s top diplomat in the city, and local officials.
“What we want to do is to strengthen those ties across our business, across education and people,” she said in a media briefing on Friday.
“But constructive engagement does not mean avoiding difficult issues, and we will always speak candidly where we have concerns. The UK will continue to stand up for the rule of law and the rights and freedoms that have underpinned Hong Kong’s success.”
Winterton serves as the parliamentary undersecretary of state for Indo-Pacific at the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.

Her trip came against the backdrop of a thaw in China-UK relations, following a visit by former British prime minister Keir Starmer to Beijing in January and a call last month between Chinese President Xi Jinping and current British leader Andy Burnham, in which Xi called for deeper cooperation.
“We believe very strongly that Hong Kong’s success is in Britain’s interest, just as Britain’s economic engagement is in Hong Kong’s interest,” Winterton said.
“Our economic connections with Hong Kong are significant. As an important international financial centre and one of the UK’s top 20 trading partners, there are some real opportunities to deepen trade, investment and business cooperation.”
Winterton toured the Hong Kong-Shenzhen Innovation and Technology Park in the Lok Ma Chau Loop. She met officials from the Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau and global pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca, which has a presence at the park, to discuss expanding scientific and technological collaboration.
Winterton also met with Undersecretary for Commerce and Economic Development Bernard Chan Pak-li as well as Cui, the commissioner of the Chinese foreign ministry’s office in the city.
According to a statement from the British consulate, both sides discussed “key aspects of the UK-China relationship”.
Winterton raised the impact of national security laws on rights and freedoms in Hong Kong, including the case of Lai.
Lai, founder of the now-defunct Apple Daily tabloid newspaper, was sentenced to 20 years in prison in February for violating the national security law.
Winterton also visited the Admiralty Learning Centre of the University of Hong Kong School of Professional and Continuing Education and joined alumni of the Chevening Scholarship, the British government’s global flagship scholarship, on a tour at Wong Tai Sin Temple.
She held meetings with senior business leaders, investors and professional services representatives to discuss opportunities in Hong Kong for British companies.
Winterton’s trip follows several earlier visits by her predecessor, former Indo-Pacific minister Catherine West. West travelled to Hong Kong in November 2024 and met with Chief Secretary Eric Chan Kwok-ki, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po and Cui.
West made another trip to Hong Kong in May last year to strengthen bilateral relations.

data.title: Hong Kong primary pupils to study AI under new technology subject
data.description:
A new subject called information and innovation technology (IIT) will be introduced gradually in Hong Kong primary schools from September 2028 to boost students’ digital literacy, with artificial intelligence (AI) one of its highlights.
Students as young as seven will be able to hold simple “conversations” with an AI system, using simple prompts or commands, after learning about the technology.
The Education Bureau said the aim of the “Information and Innovation Technology Curriculum Framework for Primary Schools (Provisional Draft)”, announced on Friday, was to enhance students’ curiosity and interest in learning innovation technology, as well as their digital literacy and creativity.
Pupils will have one 35-minute IIT lesson a week from Primary One to Six, with at least 28 classes or 16 hours for each grade – a total of 168 lessons across six years.
The subject will be introduced gradually, beginning with Primary One and Primary Four in the 2028-29 school year, with full implementation in 2030-31.
But the bureau said schools that were adequately prepared could also fully implement the curriculum in the 2028-29 school year. Schools may also pilot its content in the next school year.
It said it would provide a series of support measures for schools and teachers, including two briefing sessions on the curriculum framework next month.

William Lam Wai-lim, the bureau’s principal education officer, said the experiences of different countries and regions, including mainland China, in science and technology education had been referenced when drafting the curriculum.
“In the age of AI, students not only need to master information technology knowledge and skills from a young age, but also need to cultivate digital literacy including media and information literacy and AI literacy, the abilities required for human-computer collaboration, and correct values and attitudes,” he wrote in the bureau’s online blog, Insider’s Perspectives.
The new subject will cover five strands: information technology concepts and applications; computational thinking and coding; AI; fundamental engineering and robotics technology; and technology and society.
AI and computational thinking and coding will each account for 41 of the 168 lessons.
The draft said schools should guide students to understand that AI is merely an auxiliary tool and avoid over-relying on it to the extent of “outsourcing their thinking”.
Primary One pupils, some as young as six, should be able to understand the concept of “input-processing-output” through everyday examples, such as a juicer, a toaster, a rice cooker and taking pictures.
They are expected to recognise and use common internet applications, such as email, search engines and streaming platforms. It is suggested that they learn how to use search engines to find specific information.
Primary Two students will start studying the AI module, according to the draft.
These pupils, who are as young as seven, are expected to cite some examples of AI applications, understand the concepts of intelligence and conduct simple conversations with AI systems using simple prompts or instructions under teachers’ guidance.
Senior primary students will learn more advanced AI concepts, such as generative AI.
In Primary Five, pupils will learn to write complete prompts following a basic structure. They are encouraged to use prompt frameworks to create story illustrations, brief descriptions, posters and other materials.
They also are to understand the relationship between computing power, chip technology and tokens and the three key elements of AI: data, algorithms and computing power.
In Primary Six, students are to compose prompts independently to accomplish tasks. It is suggested they design and test prompts and compare the impact of different writing styles on the results generated by AI to meet the needs of different tasks.
They should also know AI may produce erroneous, biased results and judgments and recognise their impacts, such as AI hallucinations.
The bureau also said the new subject would not be included in the Primary Five and Six internal assessments, a series of exams whose scores determine students’ secondary school placement rankings.
Teachers can submit their views on the draft through a survey by December 2.

data.title: Hong Kong development chief denies U-turn over agency to support homeowners
data.description:
Hong Kong’s development chief has rejected accusations of a policy U-turn over the establishment of a dedicated agency to help flat owners with building repair tenders, insisting the agency’s planned remit differs fundamentally from one rejected a decade ago.
Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho, in a press conference on Friday, elaborated on the scope of work of the Building Maintenance Support and Services Council, which will be established by the end of this year. She was asked if this contradicted an earlier statement from the government.
“I have reservations about establishing an independent building maintenance authority. I have always had reservations about combining law enforcement with support and assistance, as there is an inherent contradiction between the two,” she said.
“[If] the independent body [the council] provides the support, while regulation and law enforcement remain with the Buildings Department, then what is being proposed today does not present any major conflict with my view.”
As part of an overhaul to ensure renovation professionals and contractors were qualified, the government proposed setting up the council to recommend qualified contractors from among bidders.
The council, which would be established as a government-owned company by this year, would have no statutory power. However, homeowners will be required to follow its recommendations if they want to receive subsidies.
The Buildings Department will continue to oversee renovation projects in Hong Kong.




In 2015, a landmark bid-rigging case sparked calls for the government to set up an independent body to assist homeowners during bids for building renovation projects. In the case, contractor Yau Shui-tin pleaded guilty to conspiracy to offer an advantage concerning a project at Garden Vista in Sha Tin. Demand for the new body was backed by a broad spectrum of lawmakers, civil alliances and professional groups.
The then secretary for development, Eric Ma Siu-cheung, brushed aside the idea, saying that it was more “direct and effective” for separate bodies – including police, the Independent Commission Against Corruption and the Competition Commission – to handle cases under their powers.
“Building maintenance also involves building management matters. An independent body would also find it hard to intervene in disputes among owners over maintenance,” he told lawmakers in 2015.
Ma also stressed that setting up an independent body would inevitably involve administrative costs, which would “very likely be passed on to owners”, pushing up the cost of maintenance works.

Advocates for homeowners at that time included Vincent Ho Kui-yip, a former president of the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors, who now chairs its Task Force on Building Repair, Maintenance, Alteration and Addition.
Ho said on Friday that the government’s plan aligned closely with the proposal put forward in 2015, although the campaigners had hoped a statutory body would be established.
However, he believed that the government’s legislative amendments to give enforcement agencies more powers during investigations and the internal overhaul of the Buildings Department would create a more solid “safety net” for homeowners.
Commenting on why reforms took nearly a decade to materialise, Ho noted that social sentiment had shifted in the wake of last year’s deadly fire in Tai Po.
“I have often asked myself: if the government had pursued our recommendations back then, would authorities have committed such substantial public resources? It required the right sentiment for the public to become receptive,” Ho said.
“Today, the public understands that the costs incurred by government intervention are worthwhile. You end up losing less money to unscrupulous syndicates. Most importantly, it guarantees construction quality and safeguards your own safety and assets.”
Winfield Chong Wing-fai, a former Democratic Party member and a core member of the Property Owners Anti-bid Rigging Alliance, also campaigned for an independent watchdog in 2015.
He said that at that time, demand for a government entity stemmed from frustration among flat owners who found themselves “hitting a brick wall” whenever they lodged complaints with disjointed government departments.
He suspected that this problem would remain if the planned remit of the new body focused primarily on providing support services.
“At that time, we felt the government should model an entity after the Small Claims Tribunal or the Labour Tribunal – a dedicated body to adjudicate building management disputes,” he said.
“Even if you cannot immediately catch the criminal syndicates, you at least have a platform to resolve bitter disputes between owners.”
Vincent Ho Kui-yip is a candidate for the Election Committee Subsector (ECSS) Ordinary Elections 2026. A full list of candidates can be viewed here.

data.title: Hong Kong ministers defend decision not to resign over deadly Tai Po fire
data.description:
Ministers have defended their decision not to step down over the deadly Tai Po fire, insisting they are putting Hong Kong’s well-being ahead of personal considerations.
A senior official also hinted that a successor might not be named to replace Winnie Ho Wing-yin, who resigned as housing minister to take political accountability for the city’s deadliest disaster in decades.
Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun, who is now serving as acting housing minister, apologised alongside three cabinet colleagues on Friday as they unveiled details of reforms aimed at preventing a repeat of the tragedy.
The officials were Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung, Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho and Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah.
All but Yau joined Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu at Thursday’s press briefing, where top officials bowed and apologised for the fire that killed 168 people in November last year.
“I have thought on this … the chief executive previously used the analogy at a Legislative Council meeting that he was the captain of a ship, and then I would be a crew member on that voyage,” Linn said when asked whether she had considered stepping down.
“Sometimes it is not about personal wishes or considerations. I need to have discipline and follow the captain’s instructions.”

Linn added that as a team member, she had the responsibility to do her job well.
When Tang was asked repeatedly whether he would join Ho in resigning, he said his own views on the matter were “not important”.
“Society is important, Hong Kong is important, the country is important,” he said.
Tang explained that the chief executive had demanded reforms and “result-oriented governance”.
Deputy Financial Secretary Wong said Lee had given clear instructions to officials to remain in their posts, learn from the tragedy and ensure such a disaster would not happen again.
Lee had also explained his considerations to the public and was the “decision maker” on political accountability, Wong said.
In an earlier statement on her departure, Ho said: “I hope the deceased may rest in peace, and that their families may find peace to move forward and recover from their grief as soon as possible.”
The reform measures showed that the government would not shy away from difficulties and was determined to tackle long-standing problems, she said. No personal wrongdoing by Ho has been found.
Wong said no end date had been set for his interim tenure as housing chief.
“At present, the acting arrangement is open-ended,” he said.
“The chief executive will give it further consideration. However, as everyone is aware, there are only about eight months remaining in the current government’s term. Whether a suitable person can be found within eight months is indeed a challenge,” he said.
Wong added that he was prepared to serve in the role for either a long or short period.
The Housing Bureau had made notable progress, such as boosting the supply of public flats, he said, while also expressing hope that the public would recognise the accomplishments.
Asked if the government was seeking to diminish the Housing Bureau’s role in the blaze by calling on the public to recognise its achievements, Wong said it was “not a zero-sum game,” insisting the tragedy did not diminish the bureau’s track record.
“In all my sincerity and honesty, there were many positive achievements [of the Housing Bureau] that should be considered,” he said.

data.title: Hong Kong’s planned renovation body may be liable for poor oversight: minister
data.description:
Hong Kong’s planned renovation monitoring body could be held liable for poor oversight when recommending and keeping tabs on consultants and contractors, Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho has warned, as officials detailed broader reforms to curb malpractice during major building repairs.
Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun on Friday also gave assurances that a new department overseeing major renovation projects would adopt a fresh approach and provide training, despite being staffed by personnel from the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit (ICU) – the agency with the biggest responsibility for the city’s deadliest fire in Tai Po.
The officials’ remarks followed a second public apology from the ministers implicated in the inferno, with authorities vowing to have enforcement agencies sit in “high-risk” owners committee meetings and criminalise bid-rigging by next April.
Wong said he hoped a raft of reforms proposed by the government could help build a healthy environment for effective building renovations.
“Previously, our system relied on trust in the professionals … Today, we have found a group of black sheep among the professionals from the incidents. We need to adjust and strike a balance,” he said.
“In the future, we will leverage the professionals’ technical skills and knowledge, but we need robust regulation.”
As part of an overhaul, the government proposed setting up a body, known as the Building Maintenance Support and Services Council, to recommend qualified professionals and contractors. Buildings Department will also supervise some procedures.
Under the operation, the council will assign inspection consultants to owners and monitor the inspection process. The department will conduct surprise checks and review the inspection report submitted by the consultant. The report has to be approved by the department.
The council will recommend up to three contenders for each supervision consultant and contractor tender exercise, and handle declarations of interest from professionals, companies and the management committees of the owners’ corporations.
Owners must appoint consultants and contractors from the three recommendations to receive government subsidies for renovation works.
Currently, building maintenance projects enjoy a simplified approval process. But under the new regime, professionals must submit detailed documents, including building plans and a supervision proposal, to apply for a maintenance work permit.
During renovations, the council will request regular progress reports from the supervision consultant and provide independent advice to owners if the renovation requires higher costs or the work scope changes significantly.
The supervision consultant has to submit a report to the department every six months, while the department will inspect sites with major maintenance at least once every six months.
The department will also conduct random checks on the project completion reports.

But development chief Linn noted the council’s services would not be free as homeowners had the “primary responsibility” for building maintenance. She estimated that the renovation would cost several thousand Hong Kong dollars for each household, up from a few hundred.
Asked if the council would be held accountable in case issues arise, Linn said it was not a straightforward answer, as violation of the contractual provision would be dealt with between owners, professionals and contractors.
But she said the council could be liable, given its role in overseeing the performance of consultants and contractors.
“In case the council is being lax in its monitoring duty, the council will have a role and liability,” she said.
The council would have civil liabilities under the service contract if it overlooked crucial matters when recommending certain consultants or contractors, she explained.
While the council will be a company owned by the government, rather than a statutory body, Linn said its staff would still be penalised in case of misconduct, such as dismissal.
Authorities also planned to increase penalties for professionals. For instance, the offence of carrying out inspections or works that cause injury or damage will be increased from a HK$1 million (US$127,450) fine and three years’ imprisonment to HK$10 million and five years behind bars.
Wong, who also serves as the acting housing minister, detailed how the ICU would be replaced with the Public Housing Building Control Section next month, with the ICU’s roughly 300 staff being transferred to the section.
Questioned if the restructuring would just be a “cosmetic reform”, Wong brushes aside concerns.
According to Wong, the control section will operate based on work projects, rather than the current regulatory teams, to handle major maintenance works at individual estates.
He said it would also step up communication with the Buildings Department, which oversees works at private properties, from once a year to at least once a quarter, adding that staff training would be provided to increase their awareness.
“We think these changes will help improve our future services significantly,” he said.
Vincent Ho Kui-yip, chairman of the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors’ Task Force on Building Repair, Maintenance, Alteration and Addition, said the council should have an internal mechanism to monitor staff performance to ease public concerns.
He added that the council would also collaborate with enforcement agencies to vet contractors and consultants before allowing them to join tenders.
Ho believed that the mechanism would at least filter out most bad actors and monitor industry players to prevent misconduct.
Ho is a candidate for the Election Committee Subsector Ordinary Elections 2026. A full list of candidates can be viewed here.

data.title: Hong Kong artist dismayed as works stolen hours before exhibition due to open
data.description:
Hong Kong police are investigating the suspected theft of five styrofoam sculptures created by local artist Keith Lam Yan-kit. The sculptures were discovered missing from Hong Kong City Hall in Central hours before the opening of a major new exhibition.
At just after 2.30pm on Friday afternoon, officers received a report from the Microwave International New Media Arts Festival 2026 about the missing art pieces, which are part of an eight-piece work. The case has been classified as theft and assigned to the Central district crime investigation team.
An officer from the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) at the scene said a carton containing five of the eight pieces intended for the exhibition was understood to have been delivered to the venue earlier. The carton subsequently disappeared, and police would coordinate with City Hall management to review CCTV footage as they tried to trace the missing items.
According to a police source, the five artworks were last seen on Wednesday afternoon, when exhibition staff moved them into the venue ahead of installation. Their disappearance was discovered on Friday as staff prepared to put the pieces on display.
The source said that after installation work from 9am and 8pm, City Hall staff closed the exhibition hall’s entrances and exits – the only areas covered by CCTV cameras.

The stolen artworks were insured for their production fee of HK$160,000 (US$20,500), including the original machine used to create them. Lam, currently an artist-in-residence at the National Asian Culture Center in South Korea, was profoundly dismayed by the incident.
“I am really sad. It’s such an important work. I started the series in 2013. It was after a few years when I felt a bit lost artistically and I found my direction again with this work,” he said.
“Because I used real-time online data to make these blocks, they cannot ever be remade. Microwave is an extremely important festival for me and that makes me doubly sad.”
The work – One Day Social Sculpture – could be seen partially installed in one of the rooms at the venue. Eight shelves are hanging on a wall, each with a date from 2013 to 2014 underneath it. The three unstolen pieces of the work are resting on the shelves. The jagged styrofoam pieces were made by a machine using real-time social media data to carve them into blocks.
Lam said the idea came from the famous conceptual artist Joseph Beuys’ quote – “Everyone is an artist” – and was based around the notion of creating sculptures from society.
Lam said that he could see no political motive behind the incident, adding that stealing five out of the eight pieces would not make much of a financial return on the black market.
The sculptures were to be featured in the festival’s main exhibition, The Science of Immateriality, which opens on Saturday and runs until November 8.
Curated by Joel Kwong, the exhibition explored the intersection of technology, data, and intangible realities, examining how digital concepts manifest in physical spaces.
The Microwave Festival, which marks its 30th anniversary this year, focuses on bringing forward-looking, technology-driven media art to Hong Kong and on challenging audiences to reflect on contemporary societal themes.

data.title: Security chief vows his task force will root out bid-rigging in Hong Kong
data.description:
Hong Kong’s security chief has expressed confidence that a new joint task force led by him will eradicate the decades-long problem of bid-rigging, while denying that the reforms came too late after the deadly Tai Po fire.
Secretary for Security Chris Tang Ping-keung also said on Friday that law enforcement officers would attend meetings of owners’ corporations where the risk of bid-rigging was deemed high to gather frontline intelligence and intervene early.
Authorities also hope to pass new legislation criminalising bid-rigging by April next year.
In response to the damning report by a judge-led independent committee investigating the fire at Wang Fuk Court last year, Tang’s task force will combine intelligence and enforcement powers from police, the Independent Commission Against Corruption and the Competition Commission to combat bid-rigging.
Representatives from the three bodies would strengthen their intelligence sharing about syndicates and cases, enhancing analysis to identify suspicious cases early, Tang said.
“The task force will set up a dedicated operational mechanism targeting bid-rigging syndicates to enhance intelligence gathering and exchange, joint enforcement operations and risk alerts to safeguard fair competition in the market and protect the public interest,” he said.
The intelligence sharing would allow the three agencies to engage at an earlier stage of investigations, with each bringing its own database to increase efficiency and uncover the masterminds behind bid-rigging syndicates, Tang explained.
“The government is determined, confident and capable of combating bid-rigging, which is an act that seriously hurts the public’s and homeowners’ interests,” the minister said.
Tang said that following the fire, the government had concluded a comprehensive review of what the panel called a “legacy of poor practice”.




“We realise some of these companies might reach out to homeowners when they know the buildings are going to undergo major renovations, purchase flats to become owners and send their staff to become owners’ corporation members,” he said.
“Sometimes directors of companies are the same among contractors and consultants. With the task force, we will share intelligence more efficiently and combat bid-rigging.”
The proposed legislative amendments, law enforcement coordination and frontline prevention would plug loopholes enabling bid-rigging and the criminal activities of syndicates, he said.
“The aim is to eradicate these malpractices and remove the chance for them to exist,” he said.
Tang added that the task force would review its effectiveness in a year, noting that the government worked on problems and sought solutions “every single day”.
Asked whether efforts to crack down on bid-rigging came too late given how long residents had complained about it, Tang stressed that authorities had always been working on this front but the task force – which allows intelligence sharing – would help.
To those involved in bid-rigging, he vowed that the task force would hunt them down, warning: “You no longer have a chance.”


Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah said the government would amend the Competition Ordinance to criminalise anticompetitive conduct in building maintenance tenders, including bid-rigging.
Authorities would also bring the new offence under the Organised and Serious Crimes Ordinance and the Independent Commission Against Corruption Ordinance to strengthen the powers of enforcement agencies.
The proposed amendments target bid-rigging, price fixing, market exploitation and output restrictions. Both individuals and companies could be held criminally liable.
The proposed maximum penalty is 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of HK$10 million (US$1.3 million), or alternatively three times the gains derived from the contravention or 50 per cent of a company’s local turnover for each year of the offence.
Rasul Butt, CEO of the Competition Commission, said he hoped the new legislation would be discussed in the Legislative Council “very soon”.
“In terms of going to Legco to seek approval to pass the new amendments, the aim right now is April next year,” he said.

data.title: Beijing rejects spy claims involving Nvidia CEO amid rising US-China tech tensions
data.description:
China on Friday hit out at reported US intelligence allegations that a suspected Chinese spy had targeted Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, dismissing the claims as “groundless speculation” aimed at smearing Beijing.
“The relevant report is based on groundless speculation and [is] purely aimed at smearing and slandering China,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular media briefing in Beijing.
The pushback came after US outlet The New York Times reported on Thursday that US intelligence agencies had identified a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, as a suspected Chinese asset who had approached and tried to develop a close business relationship with the Nvidia chief.
US agencies believed that Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, had been passing information to Beijing, according to the report. The two Huangs are not related.
Megaspeed had previously come under US scrutiny over suspicions that the company was helping China circumvent US export controls on advanced semiconductors, the report said, citing anonymous officials with access to classified intelligence.
The news report also said US officials initially believed Nvidia’s Huang was unaware of the woman’s alleged intelligence activities, while no evidence showed that the Nvidia chief had knowingly shared sensitive information with her.

The allegations come amid heightened US scrutiny of chip exports to China, as Washington seeks to restrict Beijing’s access to premium chips critical to training advanced artificial intelligence models, citing national security concerns.
In a statement to the South China Morning Post on Friday, an Nvidia representative said that “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers” and that “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected”, as meetings with customers were part of a CEO’s job.
The company added that “the diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year”, according to the statement.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.
Once a major market for Nvidia, China has become increasingly difficult for the US chip giant to navigate, as Washington’s tightening export controls on advanced AI chips have severely restricted its sales to the country.
Meanwhile, Chinese chipmakers from Huawei Technologies to Moore Threads, among others, are gaining ground on Nvidia as Beijing accelerates efforts to achieve semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Beijing-based Moore Threads, often hailed as China’s “little Nvidia”, reported on Wednesday a nearly 1,774 per cent surge in third-quarter revenue to 1.55 billion yuan (US$232.4 million). It attributed the gain to robust domestic demand for graphics processing units used for AI model training and inference across cloud providers, telecommunications operators and computing centres.

data.title: Hong Kong to be exclusive Vinexpo Asia host from 2027 to 2031
data.description:
Hong Kong will be the exclusive host of Vinexpo Asia from 2027 to 2031, ending the international wine and spirits trade exhibition’s rotation with Singapore.
The organiser of the fair, Vinexposium, confirmed its five-year commitment to the city on Friday, signing a memorandum of understanding with the Hong Kong Tourism Board (HKTB).
HKTB chairman Peter Lam Kin-ngok called the strategic partnership a milestone that underscored a commitment to strengthen Hong Kong’s position as Asia’s leading destination for wine, spirits and culinary experiences.
“[Vinexposium’s] commitment is a powerful endorsement of Hong Kong’s unique advantage as an international trade centre, a superconnector between east and west and one of the world’s leading destinations for wine events,” Lam said.
“More importantly, it shows the confidence that global business and event organisers continue to place in Hong Kong.”
Lam added that the new collaboration aimed to draw more high-value visitors to the city.

Fabien Robert, a deputy mayor of the world-renowned wine-producing region of Bordeaux, was in Hong Kong to witness the signing of the deal as a representative of the region’s chamber of commerce and industry.
“It’s not a simple thing. It’s a long-term vision and long-term commitment,” he said, describing the new commitment as a marker of the stability and continuity that are essential in business.
Deborah Sanchez, Vinexposium’s overseas events director, said that after a few demanding years, she observed “strong, encouraging signs of recovery” in Hong Kong and a stabilisation of the mainland Chinese market.
“Seeing this momentum, we made a clear and decisive choice for the future: Vinexpo Asia will take place from June 8 to 10, 2027. And from now on, Hong Kong is our permanent annual home,” she said.
“By establishing Vinexpo Asia here as an annual, permanent gathering, we are giving our exhibitors and international buyers a clear, reliable anchor to plan ahead, invest and grow together.”
The most recent edition of Vinexpo Asia was held at Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre (HKCEC) in May.
It welcomed 14,273 professional participants from 76 markets, alongside 1,192 exhibitors from 38 countries and regions and facilitated 4,241 pre-booked meetings, bringing businesses, buyers and decision-makers together, Sanchez said.
“These results are not simply statistics. They reflect the confidence that the industry places in Vinexpo Asia, and the role that Hong Kong continues to play as a place where international business, knowledge and relationships converge,” she added.
According to the Hong Kong Trade Development Council, the city imported wine worth HK$4.7 billion in the first eight months of this year, marking a 16.2 per cent growth, with re-exports up eight per cent increase to HK$1.1 billion.

data.title: 8 companies apply for Hong Kong ride-hailing licences ahead of deadline
data.description:
Eight companies have applied for licences to provide ride-hailing services in Hong Kong under the new regulatory regime ahead of Friday’s deadline, the Transport Department has confirmed.
US-based Uber, Singapore-based Tada, Amap and Didi Chuxing, all of which currently serve the market, confirmed to the South China Morning Post that they had submitted applications.
Amap is operated by Alibaba Group Holding, which owns the SCMP.
“Drawing on its global operational experience and local track record, Uber will work closely with the government to implement the regulatory requirements,” Uber said in a statement.
Didi said it would support the roll-out of Hong Kong’s ride-hailing regulatory framework.
“Didi will actively cooperate with the approval process and continue to advance various preparatory work to support the smooth implementation of Hong Kong’s ride-hailing regulatory system,” it said.

The company added that the number of newly registered taxi drivers on its platform had risen by more than 35 per cent over the past three months compared with the preceding three months.
Amap, one of mainland China’s largest service providers, said it was confident it could provide quality services and would comply with the regulatory regime to offer safe, convenient and diversified services.
Singapore’s Tada also confirmed it had submitted an application.
In May, Hong Kong authorities capped the number of ride-hailing vehicle permits at 10,000, marking a key step in their long-running effort to regulate the market.
The Transport and Logistics Bureau announced nine key requirements for ride-hailing operators in late August, with licence applications closing on October 30. The first batch of applications is expected to be approved in late November or early December.

Among the requirements, operators must have a proven track record of providing lawful services in cities with populations of more than 7.5 million and handling more than 100,000 daily orders in at least two locations.
Operators must also submit audited financial reports for the past three years. They must have at least HK$50 million (US$6.3 million) in capital, at least HK$30 million in bank deposits and a credit line of HK$30 million.
Transport minister Mable Chan said previously that authorities had not set a quota for operator licences and would assess applicants on merit and their ability to meet the requirements.
The SCMP has contacted the Transport Department for comment.

data.title: After brutal sell-off, what comes next for the titans of Big Tech?
data.description:
Soaring artificial intelligence revenues have failed to shield Intel, Amazon and Google’s parent company Alphabet from a brutal Wall Street sell-off, as their latest quarterly results deepened investor jitters over mounting capital spending and delayed returns.
Intel plunged about 23 per cent in extended trading on Thursday, while Amazon shed 7.3 per cent. Alphabet tumbled 12.6 per cent during the regular session in its worst day on record, dragging the Nasdaq Composite down 1.4 per cent and sliding slightly further after hours.
Their earnings reports exposed the precarious economics of the AI boom: hyperscalers are racing to build out advanced computing capacity well before those assets generate enough cash to finance the next wave of infrastructure.
With both Alphabet and Amazon signalling even larger capital expenditure in 2027, any slower-than-expected top-line growth threatens to squeeze liquidity while depreciation and operational costs pile up.
Ahead of the financial results, Melissa Otto, global head at S&P Visible Alpha Research, warned on Wednesday that cloud giants’ spending was “projected to outpace revenue growth in the near term”, potentially weighing on free cash flow.
Alphabet burns cash despite cloud surge
Alphabet’s Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to US$30.7 billion, while group operating profit rose by 30 per cent. But capital expenditure of US$51.4 billion outpaced operating cash flow of US$42.3 billion, leaving a quarterly free cash outflow of US$9.1 billion.
